percentage_note: no percentage was moved by the planning documents or the ADRs. The single change in this snapshot is virtual_memory 45 -> 50: unmapping now returns the frames the space owns (ownership bit), an address space is destroyed with its private chain and its slot, and the slot is reused with a generation; each of those has a host test. The interrupt registry, the single tick source and the capability destruction are recorded as implementation evidence inside their subsystems but did not move the percentage, because their execution paths have never run. scheduler 55 -> 60 in the follow-up of the same day: its policy now runs in the host suite (12 tests) and writing them closed three preemption defects; the lock, the per-CPU ownership and the idle task remain open, so it is not higher. scheduler 60 -> 62 in the third follow-up of the day: the policy moved into a pure module (K3 step 2), a wait queue with deadlines and a mutex with ownership and direct handoff exist with 21 tests, but nothing in the kernel calls them yet and the scheduler still has no lock, which is why the move is two points and not more. scheduler 62 -> 68 in the fourth follow-up of the day: the state lock with per-CPU ownership and the generic blocking primitive exist with host tests (including a four-thread contention test), but no AP has ever run and the mutex has no user in the kernel, so it is not higher.

interrupt-line registry (kernel/arch/x86_64/interrupt_registry.zig): one owner per line, second registration refused, unregister, per-line counters, unhandled-line accounting
the kernel registers the 8254 line and the PS/2 line before interrupts are enabled; the dispatcher no longer hard-codes the vector meanings
single tick source: timer.TickSource + selectTickSource, both interrupt paths ask the policy before they count or preempt
the local APIC timer is calibrated and left disarmed while the 8254 owns the tick

the ownership of the tick is per processor: timer.CpuClock (system or local), armCpuClock refusing a contradictory role, drivesSchedulerOn answering per CPU, and an ignored-tick counter that turns a wrong clock from an opinion into a number

per-CPU segment: 8 task state segments with their own rsp0 and ist1, 8 tables (one descriptor set per base address), 8 double-fault stacks of 16 KiB, and segment.installForCpu(cpu, stack_top) which builds the table, loads the GDT and reloads the data and code segments
the entry of an AP (kynox_ap_entry) installs the segment of its CPU before it enters its loop, and the scheduler writes rsp0 through segment.tssFor(smp.cpuId())

four vectors the kernel invents have a gate, a stub and a handler: the local timer (64), the reschedule IPI (65), the TLB shootdown (66) and the halt IPI (67); the hardware range (32..47) is the other group

the device vector space (68..254, 187 vectors, the spurious 255 excluded) has one entry point per vector in assembly and a table the kernel indexes (kynox_device_stub_table), because the stub is what tells the handler which vector arrived; a shared stub would report the same number for all of them
interrupt.verify() at boot also rebuilds the gate address of the first and the last device vector and compares them with the stub table, and the kernel stops when they disagree

a device vector allocator (kernel/arch/x86_64/vector_pool.zig): a driver asks for a block of N and receives a base, N must be a power of two and the base a multiple of N (the two rules of the MSI Message Control field), the block must end before the spurious 255, the largest block is 64 because the range of 187 cannot align 128, MSI-X takes one vector per entry instead of a block, install is all or nothing, and release checks the grant before freeing anything
the boot reports how many device vectors are free for drivers, and the MSI-X report says whether the pool has one vector per table entry to give

implemented: CPU table built from the MADT enabled processors (order preserved, duplicates skipped, max_cpus cap)
BSP identified by APIC id; cpuId() translates the local APIC id through the table
AP stacks, trampoline and the INIT-SIPI-SIPI path

the trampoline is copied into the page below 1 MiB that the startup IPI names, with its placement validated against the firmware memory map and its identity mapping installed in the kernel tables (installApTrampoline at boot)

the fields of the block are written in two steps: install (GDT base, far pointer, CR3, EFER bits of the BSP, entry address) and arm (stack and CPU number of one AP, with the ready word cleared before and written last); the offsets come from the symbols of ap_trampoline.s and are validated against the size of the block

one numbering for the CPUs: the index in the CPU table that comes from the MADT indexes the stacks, is passed to the AP in RDI and is what cpuId() returns; a CPU number the table cannot hold is refused before any IPI

the AP sets the EFER bits of the BSP (LME and, when the kernel enabled it, NXE) before it loads the kernel CR3: an NX entry with NXE clear is a reserved bit that faults inside the trampoline, where there is no IDT

an AP that reaches kynox_ap_entry installs its segment, marks itself online and enters the scheduler through a hook (smp.installCpuEntryHook): it adopts a kernel task of its own and gets the idle task of its CPU, so its queue is never empty and current[CPU] is never null

the reschedule IPI: vector 65 with its gate, its stub and its handler, apic.sendReschedule and smp.reschedule, which refuses the CPU that asks (a self-IPI can be refused by the hardware), an id the table does not have, a CPU that has not registered and a controller that is not mapped
the boot migrates the second worker to the first online AP (distributeWorkToAps), which is what gives an AP something to run: the tasks of the boot are created by the BSP
the online count of the CPU table is incremented once per processor: the AP counts itself in registerCpu, and startAps no longer counts it again

the TLB shootdown: vector 66, apic.sendShootdown, and a mailbox (kernel/arch/x86_64/tlb.zig) that carries the page because an IPI carries only a vector — a generation per request so a repeated announcement is a duplicate and a late answer is stale, and a compare-and-swap so the count of pending answers never passes below zero

smp.shootdown refuses with a reason (no_targets, no_apic, complete, timeout) and the handler runs on the processor that holds the stale entry, invalidates it (invlpg, or a reload of CR3 for the all scope) and acknowledges

a clock per processor: timer.armCpuClock gives each CPU a role (system on the BSP, local on an AP), timer.drivesSchedulerOn answers per processor, timer.onCpuTick counts per CPU and moves the clock of the machine only for the system role, and timer.ticksOf/ignoredTicks expose the numbers
an AP enables its own local APIC (enable, TPR 0) and arms its own timer with the bus frequency the BSP measured (timer.armLocalApicTimer), refusing instead of guessing when there is no measurement

the block of the APs is placed against the firmware data, not only against the memory map: kernel/arch/x86_64/bda.zig reads the EBDA segment at 0x40E, fitsBelowEbda requires the block to end at or below its base, and smp.prepareTrampoline refuses with error.OverlapsEbda

the halt IPI (vector 67): apic.sendHalt and smp.stopOtherCpus, which counts the processors that are online and the IPIs it actually delivered, and smp.describeStop, which prints those two numbers and the reason when they differ (no controller)
AP startup gated on a published trampoline and on the number of discovered processors, with a bounded wait and explicit failure reporting
limitations: no AP has ever answered a startup IPI in this environment: the copy, the fields and the order are code and host tests, not an observed second processor
no IPI has ever been delivered here: the reschedule, the shootdown and the halt are vectors, gates and handlers, and host tests of what decides what to send
an AP arms its own clock, but no AP has ever run one: the arming and the per-CPU ledger are code and host tests
no nested shootdown: the sender holds the mailbox lock while it waits, so a shootdown requested from inside another one (or from a handler) would deadlock
a shootdown that times out is counted and not retried; nothing chases the processor that did not answer
no migration of a running task
the EBDA pointer has never been read on hardware, and a firmware that publishes none falls back to the page 0x8000 as a documented assumption

implemented: timer-driven preemption
task contexts and state machine
context-switch assembly
scheduler statistics
one clock counts the tick, so the quantum and the timeout math are no longer doubled by two armed timers
EEVDF choice of the next ready task with a virtual runtime, a deadline and a weight per task
the quantum decides when a task leaves: a tick with slice left only moves the clock
the entering task gets the quantum of its slice, so time-slicing is not a once-per-lifetime event
a preemption that finds no other ready task restores the current one instead of leaving it ready
the scheduler policy covered by host tests (kernel/task_root.zig, artifact scheduler-tests)
the policy is a pure module with no globals (`task/policy.zig`): pickNext, shouldPreempt, quantumFor, budgetFor, minVruntime, tested on their own
a wait queue with FIFO order, a deadline per wait and a remembered wake, so a producer that runs before its waiter cannot lose the wakeup (task/wait.zig)
a mutex with an owner, a recursion limit and a direct handoff: the ownership moves to the waiter before the wake, so no third task can take it in the interval (task/mutex.zig)
the channel of the IPC registers its waiters in the wait queue: the queue has its first caller in the kernel, and the queue of waiters is FIFO instead of being the order of the storage array
a state lock with per-CPU ownership (owner, depth, contentions, re-entries, refused releases) taken by every entry point of the scheduler, released on every path, and counted in the boot report
blockCurrentOn: the generic blocking primitive over any wait queue, with a deadline written before the node is queued and the wait undone when there is nobody to switch to

an idle task created at boot by Scheduler.ensureIdle (idempotent, reported as Statistics.idle): a ring 3 task whose body halts the processor with sti; hlt, with 8 KiB of user stack and 8 KiB of kernel stack

the policy chooses the idle task only when no other task is eligible, whatever its virtual runtime (policy.Entry.idle, policy.idleVruntime), so it is the last resort of the queue and never displaces a real task
one idle task per CPU, with its own user and kernel stacks: the last resort of a processor belongs to that processor

an owner per task (Task.cpu): the choice of a CPU skips every task of another processor, so a second CPU cannot take the task, the stack or the idle task of the first; enqueueReady records the owning CPU

adoptKernelTask: an AP that arrives from the trampoline gets a kernel task of its own (ring 0, its own stack, state running) and becomes current[CPU], so prepareNext has a context to save instead of returning before it reads the queue

rescheduleCurrent: the handler of the reschedule IPI decides without counting a tick and without charging the slice (decideNext(forced)), so a timeout never depends on another CPU and a task's quantum never shrinks because somebody asked a question

migrateTo: moves a task to the queue of another CPU (refusing a running task, a terminated one, an id above max_cpus and a move to the current owner), which is the only way a task reaches a processor other than the one that created it
wakeTask queues the awakened task on the CPU that owns it and requests a reschedule of that CPU when it is another one, instead of silently migrating it to the waker's queue

the slot of a task that ended goes back to the pool: `requestReap` (from `terminateCurrent` and `killCurrent`) puts the task in an intrusive list that lives in the slot itself, and `reap` — run from the tick, never from the task being collected — releases it, with the ready queues purged first so a pointer to the slot cannot become the next task; a slot stays out while a CPU is running it or while the canary of its kernel stack does not hold, and `allocate` reuses the first hole
limitations: effectively BSP-centric: no AP has ever run, so the lock is never contended in the kernel (it is contended on the host by four threads)
the idle task is created and reported at boot, but no hlt of this tree has executed here
an AP has no clock of its own: the reschedule IPI is the only thing that can make it look at its queue, and no IPI has ever been delivered here
fairness across CPUs: nothing balances the queues, and a running task cannot be migrated
the switch to the idle task has never crossed a real context switch (the host tests stop at the decision)
the mutex has no user in the kernel yet; the end-to-end test is the proof of the chain
statisticsOf reads the state without the lock, by design (diagnostics)
no reader/writer lock, no condition variable, no futex-like primitive
no migration or fairness policy, no SMP safety proof
the assembly of the switch still does not save FPU/SSE state (audit defect 8)

a machine to observe the halt and an IPI being delivered
a user of the mutex in the kernel

per-CPU run queues with a migration protocol
the reaper has never run on a machine, there is no join/wait, and the address space of a user process that ends is never destroyed (`process.reapFull` exists and no boot path calls it)

two tick sources counted and preempted; closed in code: timer.TickSource policy, the local APIC timer stays disarmed, host tests
the arch-tests artifact did not compile, so the reported 716 tests excluded the architecture suite; closed: fpu.zig operand names and the paging import; 736 tests measured

the scheduler had no synchronisation and no tests. Closed for the code: a state lock with per-CPU ownership is taken by every entry point and released on every path (host tests, including four threads contending), the policy is a pure module with its own tests, blockCurrentOn gives the mutex its blocking primitive, the idle task is created at boot and chosen only when nothing else can run, and the segment of the CPU (rsp0, ist1, its own table) is installed by the entry of an AP. Open for the evidence: no AP has ever run, so no two processors contend in the kernel; the trampoline is now published below 1 MiB, INIT/SIPI are sent, the AP enters the scheduler with a task of its own and a reschedule IPI can wake it with work, but no AP has answered, no IPI has been delivered and the idle task has never halted here; 2026-11-08: the task-slot leak is closed in code — `Scheduler.reap` hands the slot of a terminated task back to the pool and the ready queues are purged before the slot is reused, with seven host tests; still open for the evidence: no AP, no IPI, no reaper run

the synchronisation primitives the kernel needs did not exist: no mutex with an owner, no wait queue, and a wait-queue stub whose dequeue returned a field that nothing set. A mutex (owner, recursion, direct handoff) and a wait queue (FIFO, deadlines, remembered wake) now exist with 21 host tests; no kernel path calls them yet

kernel/task/runqueue.zig was a stub that dequeued without shifting and was imported by nothing; deleted. The per-CPU ready queue of the scheduler is the real one, and it is still not safe under SMP because there is no lock

the scheduler called itself inside one decision (tick -> expiry -> wake -> enqueue) with no way to say so, which is why a plain spinlock would have deadlocked on the first tick that expired a wait; the state lock now knows its CPU and counts the re-entries instead. The counters are reported at boot

known_documentation_mismatches: kernel/arch/x86_64/virtio_blk.zig is a legacy stub returning NotImplemented; the active driver is kernel/drivers/kvdi/block.zig. Removal decided in ADR-0003, not executed.

kernel/arch/x86_64/virtio.zig duplicates the split virtqueue that KVDI actually programs, and the boot marker virtio: split queue layout ok currently proves the duplicate (ADR-0002).
kernel/arch/x86_64/virtio_blk.zig used to reference a non-existent docs/adr/ADR-F04-block-driver-proposta.md; corrected. ADRs live in docs/decisions/ per strategy.md.
